title: How Supreme Court Nominations Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how Supreme Court nominations work in the United States. They cover the Court's constitutional vagueness and the Marbury v. Madison (1803) origin of judicial review, lifetime appointments, the nominee qualifications tradition (lawyers, federal judges, clerks), the president's selection from a list, Senate hearings and the "kabuki" dance of nominees dodging questions, media digging up nominees' pasts (Harriet Miers), withdrawals and rejections (Roger Taney under Andrew Jackson), the Anita Hill and Clarence Thomas hearings, Merrick Garland's blocked nomination in 2016, the tie-vote rule, the nuclear option and filibuster, ideological measurement scores, and the political stakes of picking nominees. The episode also includes a listener email about Trail of Tears and a note about Ed Grabianowski's return to writing for the site.

entities.name: Supreme Court of the United States

segments.title: Opening banter and Ed Grabianowski announcement
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the Supreme Court's secrecy and hearings, Clarence Thomas's silence on the bench, and announce that Ed Grabianowski will write again for the site on requested topics.

segments.title: Supreme Court role and Marbury v. Madison
segments.summary: The Constitution is vague about the Court's power. The Court's role in reviewing laws under the Constitution began with Marbury v. Madison in 1803. Justices serve for life, average about fourteen years, and the Court hears roughly 100 to 150 of about 5,000 cases a year. Its rulings are final and can make similar state laws void.

segments.title: Tie votes, five-to-four decisions, and swing votes
segments.summary: With eight justices, a tie leaves the lower court decision upheld only for that case. Five-to-four decisions are common, and Kennedy is described as the swing vote, previously Sandra Day O'Connor.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the appointments discussion.

segments.title: Qualifications and presidential selection
segments.summary: There are no formal qualifications for the Court. In practice nominees are lawyers, usually federal judges, often former clerks, and sometimes politicians. Howard Taft is noted as a former president who served on the Court. The president picks from a list of candidates.

segments.title: Senate hearings, vetting, and the nominee's non-answers
segments.summary: Once a nominee is named, the Justice Department and Senate staff investigate their past. Nominees avoid stating positions on hot-button issues, which the hosts call a kabuki dance. Media reports fill in gaps; Harriet Miers was criticized after reports of a political donation and a comment calling Bush cool.

segments.title: Rejections, withdrawals, Clarence Thomas and Anita Hill, and Merrick Garland
segments.summary: Most nominations are confirmed; rejections are rare and withdrawals more common. Roger Taney was rejected and renominated under Andrew Jackson. The Clarence Thomas hearings included Anita Hill's testimony. Senate Republicans refused to hold hearings or votes on Merrick Garland in 2016, an election year, and the hosts discuss Garland's ideology.

segments.title: Filibuster, nuclear option, and political stakes
segments.summary: Democrats were delaying the Gorsuch vote, and Republicans could use the nuclear option to confirm by simple majority. The hosts discuss how presidents weigh ideology, Senate control, and midterm consequences. They also discuss judicial appointments in lower courts as an incubator for future nominees.

segments.title: Justices' ideology over time and trivia
segments.summary: Justices can shift ideologically over time, as with John Paul Stevens and David Souter. Ideological scores rank Scalia and Thomas as conservative, and Gorsuch is predicted to sit right of center. Arthur Goldberg's swearing-in and the Constitution in his desk drawer are described.

segments.title: Listener mail: Trail of Tears
segments.summary: Tiffany Waits writes about the Trail of Tears episodes and Cherokee sites in Calhoun, Georgia, and recommends the Stuff You Missed in History Class podcast.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and give social media and website contact information.
